segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ paramakaruṇāmaitrikam[ā]nasaḥ siddhācāryo dhāmapādo hi pratipādayati —
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Dhāmapāda]{p-dharma}, whose mind is full of supreme [compassion]{karuna} and [loving-kindness]{maitri}, sets forth that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the poet as the [siddha]{siddha} master [Dhāmapāda]{p-dharma}, whose mind is full of supreme [compassion]{karuna} and [loving-kindness]{maitri}, and says he sets forth 'that same meaning' (cp.47.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don) instead, and reads the name as Dharmapāda (chos pa'i zhabs).

flags.note: Where Munidatta has tam evārthaṃ, 'that same meaning' (cp.47.m1), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', as if its manuscript read tattvārtha. It also names the poet chos pa'i zhabs, Dharmapāda, for Dhāmapāda. I translate the Sanskrit.
The ā of mānasaḥ is Shastri's restoration (m[ā]nasaḥ). The sense is not in doubt.

segments.translit: kamalakuliśam ityādi | prajñopāyasamatāṃ satyākṣaramahāsukharāgānilāvārttān nābhau nirmāṇacakre caṇḍālī jvalitā mama |
segments.translation: '[Lotus]{lotus} and [vajra]{vajra}…' and so on. Through the [sameness]{samata} of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, from the whirling of the [wind]{vayu} of the [passion]{raga-passion} of true, imperishable [great bliss]{mahasukha}, [Caṇḍālī]{candali} has blazed at my navel, in the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra}.
segments.note: Munidatta paraphrases the first couplet: through the [sameness]{samata} of [wisdom and means]{prajnopaya}, stirred by the whirling wind of the passion of true, imperishable [great bliss]{mahasukha}, [Caṇḍālī]{candali} has blazed at the navel, in the [wheel of emanation]{nirmana-cakra} (cp.47.m2). He does not gloss lotus and vajra separately. The Tibetan has 'fire of passion' where his Sanskrit has 'wind of passion'.

flags.note: Where Munidatta has rāgānila, 'the wind of passion' (cp.47.m2), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'dod chags kyi me 'bar, 'the fire of passion blazes': its manuscript may have read anala, 'fire', for anila, 'wind'. The Tibetan has nothing for satyākṣara ('true, imperishable') or āvārtta ('whirling'), has yang dag par sbyor bas, 'by properly joining', for the bare accusative, and calls Caṇḍālī gtum mo'i me, 'the fire of Caṇḍālī'. I translate the Sanskrit's 'wind'.
Shastri prints āvārttāt. I read it as āvartāt, 'from the whirling', from āvarta, 'a turning, an eddy'. The Tibetan does not help here.

prajñopāyasamatāṃ is accusative, and no verb governs it. I take it as Munidatta's restatement (cp.47.m2) of the song's 'through the yoga of sameness' (samatā joeṃ) and render it 'through', as the Tibetan does (sbyor bas). mama, 'my', stands at the end of the sentence. It could also go with Caṇḍālī ('my Caṇḍālī'). I follow the Tibetan, which has 'my navel' (bdag gi lte ba).

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ vispaṣṭayati —
dāhetyādi | mahāsukharāgadāhayukto hy agniḥ | ḍombī pariśuddhāva[65ka]dhūti gṛhe lagnaḥ | tena mahāsukharāgāgninā mayā sakalaviṣayādivṛndāśrayo dagdhaḥ |
sasaharam iti — sadguruprasādād vilakṣaṇapariśodhitaṃ saṃvṛtibodhicittaṃ gṛhītvā tasya vahner ni(ni)rvāpaṇaṃ karomīti |
tathā ca dvikalpe —
caṇḍālī jvalitā nābhāv ityādi |
segments.translation:
With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes that same meaning plain:
'A burning…' and so on. The [fire]{fire} is the one joined with the burning of the [passion]{raga-passion} of [great bliss]{mahasukha}. It has caught in the [house]{house} of [Ḍombī]{dombi}, the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. With that [fire]{fire} of the [passion]{raga-passion} of [great bliss]{mahasukha} I have burned the support of the whole host of [sense objects]{visaya} and the rest.
'The [moon]{moon}': taking, by the [grace]{prasada} of the true [guru]{guru}, [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}, I put out that [fire]{fire}.
And so in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
'[Caṇḍālī]{candali} blazing at the navel…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the fire in [Ḍombī]{dombi}'s house as the fire of the passion of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, and Ḍombī as the purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}; with that fire 'I' have burned the support of all sense objects (cp.47.m3). The refrain's moon is conventional [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana} and received by the true guru's grace; with it the fire is put out.

equations.en: the fire joined with the burning of the passion of great bliss
conventional bodhicitta, purified by vilakṣaṇa and taken by the true guru's grace

citations.quoted: Caṇḍālī blazing at the navel… (caṇḍālī jvalitā nābhau)
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (which Munidatta calls the Dvikalpa), I.1.31

flags.note: Munidatta's lemma for 2b is sasaharam, 'the moon' (cp.47.m3). The printed line has saha ṣali. The Tibetan line (ri bong 'dzin pa'i chu, 'the hare-holder's water') and the Tibetan lemma (ri bong 'dzin pa) also have the moon. Both support the draft's 'moon'.

Shastri prints pariśuddhāvadhūti gṛhe as two words. Because avadhūti has a short final i, I take the two as one compound: 'in the house of Ḍombī, the purified avadhūtī'. The Tibetan reads it the same way (yongs su dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI'i khyim du). The other possible reading is 'Ḍombī is the purified avadhūtī; [the fire] has caught in the house'. The gloss on Ḍombī is the same either way.

Three differences in the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293). For 'joined with the burning' it has sred pa dang ldan pa, 'joined with craving'. For lagna, 'has caught', it has sbyong ba, 'purifies', which may be a copying error for sbyor ba, 'is joined'. For 'the fire of the passion of great bliss' it has only bde ba chen po'i me, 'the fire of great bliss'.
In vahner ni(ni)rvāpaṇaṃ, the bracketed syllable (ni) is Shastri's. Either way the sense is 'the extinguishing of the fire'. The lemma has dāha with a dental d. The song has ḍāha.
Munidatta names the work dvikalpa, 'the Dvikalpa' (cp.47.m3). I have used the glossary's approved title, Hevajra. The Tibetan has brtag pa gnyis pa, 'the Two Examinations'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena jñānavahneḥ svarūpam āha —
naukharetyādi | yathā bāhyavahnes tīvraṃ jvalanatādi dhūmādikaṃ dṛśyate tadvad ayaṃ jñānavahniḥ [na?] dṛśyate | kintu bhāvābhāvaṃ dagdhā pūrvoktasumeruśikharāgre gaganam iti mahāsukhacakre antarbhavatīti |
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of the [fire]{fire} of [knowledge]{jnana}:
'No fierce…' and so on. The fierce blaze and the rest, the [smoke]{smoke} and the rest, of an outer [fire]{fire} are seen; this [fire]{fire} of [knowledge]{jnana} is not seen like that. Rather, having burned [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, it is absorbed at the tip of the peak of [Sumeru]{pl-sumeru}, already mentioned, into 'the [sky]{gagana}', that is, into the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}.
segments.note: Munidatta contrasts the fire of knowledge with outer fire. Outer fire is seen blazing fiercely, with smoke, but this fire is not seen (cp.47.m4). Having burned being and nonbeing, it is absorbed at the tip of [Sumeru]{pl-sumeru}'s peak, in the sky, which he glosses as the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. The negative is Shastri's queried restoration; the Tibetan has it.

flags.note: The negative 'not' is Shastri's queried addition, [na?]. Without it, the sentence says the fire of knowledge is seen just as outer fire is. That contradicts the song ('no smoke is seen') and the 'rather' (kintu) that follows. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has the negative: ye shes kyi me ni mi mthong, 'the fire of knowledge is not seen'. I adopt it.

Shastri prints dagdhā, which I read as dagdhvā, 'having burned'. The Tibetan has bsreg pa. A mark (❌) stands inside anta❌rbhavati, and I read antarbhavati, 'is absorbed'. The Tibetan has thim pa, 'dissolves', and makes 'the fire' (me) the subject.

For 3a, Munidatta's lemma is naukhara and his paraphrase is tīvraṃ jvalana, 'a fierce blaze' (cp.47.m4). Both support the draft's 'fierce' for khara. The Tibetan line instead has rtswa ni 'bar ba ma yin, 'the grass does not blaze'; its lemma here is spelled rtsa. That reads khara as straw or grass (compare Bengali khaṛ, 'straw').

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadenoktārtha[ṃ] pratinirdeśayati —
dāṭai ityādi | bāhmeti sandhyācanena viṭanāḍikā bodhavyā | harir iti | mūtranāḍī | hara iti śukranāḍikā | etā dagdhā | ūrdhe lalanārasanādikāś ca | navaguṇam iti navapavanañ ca | śāsanam iti cakṣurindriyādiviṣayākhyañ ca dagdhvā sa eva rāgānalo niḥsvabhāvaṃ gataḥ |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
manamara ityādi |
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he points out again the meaning already stated:
'They [burn]{burning}…' and so on. '[Brahmā]{p-hari-hara-brahma}' is to be understood, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, as the [channel of excrement]{vitnadika}. '[Hari]{p-hari-hara-brahma}': the [channel of urine]{mutranadi}. '[Hara]{p-hari-hara-brahma}' means the [channel of semen]{sukranadika}. These are burned, and above, [lalanā]{lalana}, [rasanā]{rasana} and the rest as well. And 'the [nine qualities]{navaguna}' means the nine [winds]{vayu}. 'The [teaching]{sasana}' means what is called the [sense objects]{visaya} of the eye and the other [senses]{indriya}. Having burned these too, that same [fire]{fire} of [passion]{raga-passion} has become [without intrinsic nature]{nihsvabhava}.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}:
'The mind dies…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads Hari, Hara and Brahmā, in twilight language, as channels: Brahmā the [channel of excrement]{vitnadika}, Hari of urine, Hara of semen (cp.47.m5). These burn, with [lalanā]{lalana}, [rasanā]{rasana} and the rest above. The nine qualities are the nine winds, and the teaching is the objects of the senses. Having burned them, the fire of passion itself becomes without intrinsic nature.

equations.en: what is called the objects of the eye and the other senses

citations.work: Saraha, a dohā, perhaps from his Dohākoṣa (Munidatta names only the poet)

flags.note: Munidatta cites the verb of 4a as dāṭai, 'burns' (cp.47.m5). The printed line has phāṭai, 'bursts', and the draft keeps 'burst'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) sides with Munidatta: its line has tshig, 'burn', and its lemma has sreg pa, 'burning'. I translate his lemma as 'burn'. The reviewer should decide whether 4a stays 'burst'.

The Tibetan opens with rkang pa gnyis pas gsungs pa'i don so sor rgyas par bshad do. That says it explains in detail 'the meaning stated by the second verse'. So it calls this couplet's verse the 'second', where Munidatta has tṛtīya, 'third' (cp.47.m5), and it construes the phrase differently. Either its manuscript read dvitīya or the Tibetan is in error. By Munidatta's count, which leaves out the refrain, couplet 4 is the third verse.

The Tibetan lacks 'the nine qualities means the nine winds'. Instead it takes yon tan dgu dang yul gyi, 'the nine qualities and of the land', together as the eye faculty and the rest and what are called objects. It also makes the burned things become without intrinsic nature through the fire of passion ('dod chags kyi mes rang bzhin med par gyur pa). In the Sanskrit it is the fire itself that does so. For lalanā, rasanā 'and the rest' it has only la la nA dang ra sa nA.

The quoted words manamara can be divided two ways. As mana mara(i) they mean 'the mind dies'. As mana amara they mean 'the mind is deathless'. The Tibetan reads the second way: yid ni 'chi ba med pas, 'because the mind does not die'. I chose 'the mind dies', which suits the burning just described, but the quotation is too short to settle it. I have not identified the dohā.

cakṣurindriyādiviṣayākhyaṃ can mean 'what is called the objects of the eye faculty and the rest', which is my choice and the glossary's. It can also mean 'what is called the eye faculty and the rest, and the objects'. The Tibetan takes the second sense (mig gi dbang po la sogs pa dang yul du bshad pa rnams).

Several small points in Shastri's text. sandhyācanena is probably a slip for sandhyāvacanena, 'in twilight speech'. ūrdhe stands for ūrdhve, 'above'. A mark (❌) inside lalanārasanādi❌kāś is ignored. The anusvāra of uktārtha[ṃ] is his restoration.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena caturthānandapratyayitām āha —
dhāmetyādi | dhāmapādo hi vadati bho anadhigatamārga śrīgurucaraṇopāyena samyak kuliśābjasaṃyogo sphuṭaṃ kṛtvā sa [67]
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of conviction in the fourth [joy]{ananda}:
'[Dhāma]{p-dharma}…' and so on. [Dhāmapāda]{p-dharma} says: 'O you who have not attained the [path]{marga}, having properly made the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus} plain by means of the feet of the glorious [guru]{guru}, …'
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the last couplet as conveying conviction in the fourth [joy]{ananda} (cp.47.m6). Dhāmapāda addresses one who has not attained the path: 'having properly made the union of vajra and lotus plain by means of the glorious guru's feet…'. The Sanskrit then breaks off mid-word, because a folio of the manuscript is lost. Only the Tibetan translation continues (cp.47.m7).

flags.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit breaks off at sa (cp.47.m6). Shastri's folio number [67] follows, and the folio that carried the rest of this comment and song 48 is lost. The rest survives only in the Tibetan translation (cp.47.m7). That continuation opens with lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba, 'innate joy', so sa is probably the first syllable of sahajānanda. This is a conjecture.

Implications for 5a, where the draft has 'taking it from the guru, know it plainly'. (1) Munidatta's 'by means of the glorious guru's feet' (cp.47.m6) supports finding guru in leṅgūre (le + gure). (2) He has no word for 'taking'. (3) His sphuṭaṃ kṛtvā, 'having made plain', attaches phuṛa to the first action, not to 'know'. The Tibetan line does the same with gsal por blangs nas, 'having clearly taken'. (4) The Tibetan line has no guru at all: it has gsal por blangs nas rab tu shes.

In the Tibetan (Toh 2293), dpal gyi bla ma'i zhabs kyis ... gsal bar mdzad nas makes the glorious guru the one who makes the union plain; mdzad is honorific. It has nothing for upāya, 'means'. It renders pratyayitā as rkyen, 'condition' (dga' ba bzhi pa'i rkyen du), and bho, 'O', as kye'i.
kuliśābjasaṃyogo is nominative, but as the object of kṛtvā it should be accusative (°saṃyogaṃ). I translate it as the object.

segments.translit: lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba shes par gyis shig pa'o/ /de'i bde ba chen po chu skyes las 'ong ba nyid gang byang chub kyi sems nor bu'i rtse mor son pa bzhi pa'i dga' bas sbyangs pa nA da dang bcas pa pad+ma'i nA da la zhes te a wa d+hU ti'i lam gyis slar yang de nyid du 'gro ba'o/
segments.translation: …know [innate joy]{sahajananda}.' Its [great bliss]{mahasukha} is what comes from the [lotus]{lotus}. The [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} that has reached the tip of the [jewel]{mani}, purified by the fourth [joy]{ananda} and accompanied by [nāda]{nada}, goes 'to the [nāda]{nada} of the [lotus]{lotus}', that is, it goes back again by the [path]{marga} of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} to that very place.
segments.note: Munidatta's comment survives here only in the Tibetan translators' text, not his Sanskrit (cp.47.m7). It completes the address: know innate joy, whose great bliss comes from the lotus. Bodhicitta, having reached the jewel's tip and been purified by the fourth joy, goes back by the path of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. It does not explicitly gloss 5b's water or channels.

flags.note: This segment is not Munidatta's Sanskrit, which is lost with the missing folio (see cp.47.m6). It is the text of the Tibetan translators, Kīrticandra and Drakpa Gyaltsen (Toh 2293), and I have translated it from the Tibetan. Any reading it gives is Munidatta's only as they rendered him.

pad+ma'i nA da la zhes te, 'to the nāda of the lotus, that is', is unclear. In m4 the Tibetan uses zhes te for Sanskrit iti (nam mkha' la zhes te for gaganam iti), so the phrase may be a lemma that is then glossed. If so, it might stand for the song's pañcanāleṃ (5b), read as padma- with nāla or nāḍa ('stalk, channel') taken as nāda. That would make the gloss 'goes back by the path of the avadhūtī' explain the water rising. The Tibetan line has rtsa phran lnga, 'five minor channels'. This is a conjecture.

Implications for 5a. shes par gyis shig is an imperative, 'know!', and its object is innate joy (lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba). That supports the draft's reading of jāṇī as 'know', addressed to the listener. It also suggests that the draft's 'it' is innate joy. 'Plainly' belongs to the earlier 'having made the union plain' (cp.47.m6), not to 'know'.

The syntax is loose. 'Its great bliss ... gang' has no clear main clause, so the great bliss coming from the lotus may be meant as the bodhicitta itself. de nyid du can mean 'to that very place' (my choice) or 'into reality' (de nyid also renders tattva).

questions: 4a: Munidatta cites the verb as dāṭai, 'burns' (cp.47.m5). The Tibetan line (tshig) and its lemma (sreg pa) also have 'burn'. Only the printed phāṭai gives 'bursts'. In the comment I translated his lemma as 'burn'. Should the draft keep 'burst' with a reading flag, or follow the commentary and the Tibetan?

5a: Munidatta's 'by means of the glorious guru's feet' (cp.47.m6) supports the le + gure division, but nothing in his surviving Sanskrit or the Tibetan comment answers to le, 'taking'. His 'having made plain' (sphuṭaṃ kṛtvā, cp.47.m6) attaches phuṛa to the first action, and so does the Tibetan line (gsal por blangs nas, 'having clearly taken'). The Tibetan continuation's imperative 'know innate joy' (cp.47.m7) supports 'know'. Would 'taking it plainly from the guru, know —' be closer than 'taking it from the guru, know it plainly —'? Note that the Tibetan line has no guru.
Munidatta calls the work he quotes the Dvikalpa (cp.47.m3). I used the approved title Hevajra (tx-hevajra). Should 'Dvikalpa' become a listed variant, so that his title can stand in the translation?

3a: Munidatta's 'fierce blaze' (tīvraṃ jvalana, cp.47.m4) supports the draft's 'fierce' for khara. The Tibetan line reads the word as 'grass' (rtswa ni 'bar ba ma yin, 'the grass does not blaze'). Does the draft's 3a carry a witness flag for this?
Saraha's 'manamara…' (cp.47.m5): I chose 'the mind dies'. The Tibetan reads 'the mind does not die' (yid ni 'chi ba med pas). Can you identify the dohā to settle the division?

In cp.47.m5 I marked Hari, Hara and Brahmā one by one with the group id p-hari-hara-brahma, because Munidatta glosses each separately. Is that acceptable, or should only the full phrase carry the link?

Several keep-source-first-gloss terms (siddha, avadhūtī, bodhicitta, vilakṣaṇa, lalanā, rasanā, nāda) first appear in this song's commentary, not in its lines. The weave schema has no slot for a first-occurrence gloss, so I relied on the glossary links. Should a gloss go into the notes instead?
